tweets.text: A withdrawal that sends Ether before clearing the caller balance can be withdrawn against again. The callback runs while the stored balance is still unchanged.
Calling another contract hands it control. It can call back into yours before the first call returns, so your state must be final before that handoff happens.
Root cause: state updates placed after an untrusted call allow repeated execution. The callee re-enters while the old values are still in storage.
This is not limited to Ether transfers. Reentrancy can arise from calls to other contracts in general, and dependencies across multiple contracts also matter.
The fix is checks-effects-interactions: validate inputs and permissions, update the relevant storage state, then make external calls.

For a withdrawal, save the amount and clear the stored balance before calling the recipient, for example `balances[msg.sender] = 0;`. Then require the call to succeed so failure reverts the operation.
Also review other callable paths that share the affected state. A callback may enter through another function or a dependency rather than the one you guarded.
Does any function make an external call before it clears or updates the storage that the call's recipient could read or act on?

tweets.text: A developer assumes a contract has one variable named x. In older Solidity with inheritance, there can be two separate copies of x, and each part of the code reads its own.
Take contract A that defines x and inherits contract B that also defines a state variable x. A accesses one version and B accesses the other. Same name, two separate variables.
Local names, or inherited state-variable names in legacy Solidity, obscure which variable is accessed. In more complex contract systems this can go unnoticed and lead to security issues.
Shadowing can also occur within a single contract, when there are multiple definitions at contract and function level. The compiler can flag this with a warning that an outer variable is shadowed.
The Solidity scoping documentation shows such a case: the first assignment to x assigns the outer variable rather than the inner one. The code reads as if one thing is set, and another is.
Since Solidity 0.6.0, state variable shadowing is disallowed. A derived contract can only declare a state variable x if no visible state variable with the same name exists in any of its bases.
For older code, review storage variable layouts of contract systems carefully and remove any ambiguities. Always check compiler warnings, since they can flag the issue within a single contract.
Closing check: does any contract compiled before Solidity 0.6.0 redeclare a state variable name that a base contract already has, and do any compiler warnings report a shadowed variable?

tweets.text: An attacker moves a price with a large trade or a flash loan, then calls a protocol that reads that price, and the protocol acts on a value the market never really held.

A contract that reads price or valuation data an attacker can influence, directly or indirectly, makes decisions on incorrect values. The oracle is a trust boundary: the contract assumes the price reflects market conditions.
That trust can break through manipulation, staleness or misconfiguration. The protocol is trusting price inputs that attackers can move.
OWASP lists several forms: spot price manipulation through large trades, flash loans or just-in-time liquidity in the same block, and TWAP manipulation over short windows or low-liquidity periods.

Two more forms: stale or stuck data when freshness is not enforced, and aggregation that fails to reject outliers. Lending protocols that value collateral and decide liquidations are a typical consumer.
For mitigation, aggregate multiple sources with a median or mean and reject outliers. Use TWAPs over sufficient windows, and reject prices older than a maximum staleness threshold.
Avoid basing core prices on illiquid pools, and cap the impact of a single pool or feed. Halt sensitive operations such as borrowing and liquidations when data looks suspicious or is unavailable.

Also monitor deviations between the oracle and reference markets with automated alerts. Then grep your code for every place a price is read, and test that each one rejects a stale value and a single-pool outlier.
